latent_mechanisms.display_name: Antiphospholipid autoantibody endothelial and platelet activation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Pathogenic antiphospholipid antibodies, especially anti-beta2 glycoprotein I and lupus anticoagulant activity, activate endothelial cells, monocytes, platelets, and tissue factor pathways. This is confirmatory and contextual rather than a sufficient presentation-only observation.

Classical and terminal complement activation amplifies endothelial injury, platelet activation, and small-vessel thrombosis; complement pressure explains some refractory CAPS and response to C5 inhibition.

Infection, surgery, trauma, malignancy, pregnancy/postpartum physiology, SLE flare, or anticoagulation withdrawal supplies the acute second hit that turns APS thrombophilia into a rapidly progressive thrombotic storm.
Widespread fibrin-rich small-vessel occlusion across several organs within days; the core CAPS lesion and the main reason it mimics DIC and other TMAs while remaining APS-driven.
Concurrent venous and arterial thrombosis such as pulmonary embolism, stroke, myocardial infarction, limb ischemia, or renal vessel thrombosis; may coexist with the small-vessel CAPS lesion.

Small-vessel thrombi consume platelets and may mechanically fragment erythrocytes. CAPS can show thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, LDH elevation, and low haptoglobin, but does not require severe ADAMTS13 deficiency and is not DIC itself.

Cytokine-amplified inflammation and endothelial injury create fever, high CRP, SIRS physiology, ARDS pressure, and feed-forward coagulation activation; this overlaps clinically with sepsis but is not infection-specific.
The summed burden of renal, pulmonary, CNS, cardiac, cutaneous, adrenal, and intestinal ischemic injury. This mechanism converts thrombotic activity into organ failure and mortality risk.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Infection, surgery, obstetric complications, malignancy, SLE flare, or anticoagulation interruption can initiate SIRS-like thromboinflammation.
The second hit converts aPL-positive baseline risk into explosive small-vessel thrombosis.
Persistent aPL positivity is the autoimmune substrate, but it is confirmatory/contextual rather than sufficient ordinary presentation evidence.
Lupus anticoagulant is common in CAPS and may prolong phospholipid-dependent clotting assays in vitro despite thrombosis in vivo.
Medium/high IgG anticardiolipin titers support APS/CAPS context.
Anti-beta2 glycoprotein I antibodies are mechanistically central because beta2GPI-bound antibodies activate endothelium and complement.
aPL-bound endothelial and trophoblast surfaces can amplify complement activation.
Complement consumption may lower C3 in a subset of active CAPS patients.
Classical pathway activation may lower C4, especially in SLE-associated CAPS.
Terminal complement activation promotes platelet activation and endothelial thrombogenicity.
CAPS often presents with fever/SIRS physiology, especially when infection or lupus flare triggered.
CRP may be high from inflammatory trigger, tissue injury, or infection overlap.
SIRS, pain, hypoxemia, and shock physiology can drive tachycardia.
Severe CAPS may develop shock from SIRS, cardiac injury, bleeding, adrenal hemorrhage, or sepsis trigger.
Small-vessel occlusion is the defining event process of CAPS.
Platelets are consumed in widespread thrombi; thrombocytopenia is common but may be less profound than TTP.
Small-vessel fibrin thrombi can shear erythrocytes and produce TMA-like hemolysis.
Microangiopathic hemolysis creates schistocytes when the TMA component is active.
Hemolysis and bleeding/critical illness can lower hemoglobin.
LDH reflects hemolysis and ischemic organ injury.
Intravascular hemolysis consumes haptoglobin.
Hemolysis can raise indirect bilirubin.
Widespread fibrin turnover can raise D-dimer, but CAPS is not identical to consumptive DIC.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: in vitro prolongation when lupus anticoagulant is present; heparin also prolongs APTT after treatment begins
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Lupus anticoagulant can prolong phospholipid-dependent clotting time while the patient remains thrombosis-prone.
Large-vessel arterial and venous thrombosis can occur concurrently with small-vessel CAPS.
Pulmonary embolism is a common large-vessel manifestation of APS/CAPS.
Arterial thrombosis can produce stroke or transient focal deficits.
Coronary macrothrombosis or microvascular coronary occlusion can produce myocardial injury.
Small-vessel occlusion across multiple vascular beds accumulates ischemic organ injury.

Renal failure raises BUN.
Renal ischemia, cortical necrosis, renal TMA, or anticoagulation can produce hematuria.
Pulmonary emboli, pulmonary microthrombosis, ARDS, or pulmonary hemorrhage lower oxygenation.
Cardiac microthrombosis or coronary thrombosis raises troponin and worsens prognosis.
Systemic hypoperfusion or bowel/limb ischemia can raise lactate.
Kidney is the most frequently involved organ in CAPS.
Pulmonary microthrombi, SIRS, and emboli can progress to ARDS-like respiratory failure.
Pulmonary capillary injury, hemorrhage, anticoagulation, and microthrombosis can coexist in severe CAPS.
Intestinal ischemia and infarction are recognized but less frequent CAPS manifestations.
Adrenal vein thrombosis or hemorrhagic infarction can produce adrenal hemorrhage and adrenal crisis.
Cutaneous and peripheral vascular thrombosis can progress from livedo and ischemic discoloration to gangrene.
CNS ischemia, hypoxemia, SIRS, or renal failure can produce encephalopathy.
CNS thrombosis may produce focal deficits or transient hemiparesis.
Pulmonary embolism, myocardial injury, or pleuro-pulmonary involvement commonly produces chest pain.
Pulmonary embolism, ARDS, pulmonary hemorrhage, and heart failure produce dyspnea.
Mesenteric ischemia, adrenal hemorrhage, renal infarction, or pancreatitis can produce abdominal pain.
Renal cortical necrosis/infarction or adrenal hemorrhage can cause flank pain.
Cutaneous vascular occlusion can manifest as livedo reticularis or livedo racemosa.
Small-vessel thrombosis can produce painful ulcers, necrosis, and retiform purpura.

Pulmonary microthrombi and inflammation can produce severe hypoxemic respiratory failure.

Severe respiratory failure is a direct short-term mortality driver.
Renal failure contributes to multiorgan failure, bleeding/toxicity constraints, and mortality.

axis_couplings.conditionality: debridement, amputation, or severe tissue necrosis
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Progressive ischemic tissue loss often requires procedures while anticoagulated.

axis_couplings.conditionality: stronger when platelet_count below 30 x 10^9/L or invasive procedures are required
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Lower platelets increase bleeding risk even though CAPS phenotype is thrombotic.
Major bleeding, pulmonary hemorrhage, adrenal hemorrhage, or ICH can directly increase mortality and limit anticoagulation.
CAPS can raise D-dimer without classic consumptive DIC; low fibrinogen plus high D-dimer should suggest DIC overlap or another process.

axis_couplings.conditionality: anticoagulant exposure, DIC overlap, liver dysfunction, or lupus anticoagulant testing context
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Coagulation times are confounded by anticoagulants and LA; they should not alone define the CAPS disease field.
The more organ systems fail simultaneously, the shorter expected survival.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Pulmonary hemorrhage, ICH, adrenal hemorrhage, severe thrombocytopenia, or urgent procedures can force reduced intensity or temporary holds.
Bleeding risk does not mean thrombosis has stopped; it changes net benefit and monitoring intensity.

side_effects.interpretation: Bleeding risk rises with full-dose anticoagulation, thrombocytopenia, procedures, pulmonary hemorrhage, or adrenal hemorrhage.
Small but serious risk, especially with severe thrombocytopenia or hemorrhagic transformation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Immediate anti-propagation therapy for active thrombotic storm, followed by long-term APS anticoagulation after stabilization.

supportive_care: ICU-level monitoring for rapidly evolving renal, pulmonary, CNS, cardiac, adrenal, bowel, skin/limb, and bleeding involvement.
Daily or more frequent CBC, platelet count, hemolysis labs, creatinine/BUN, urine sediment, PT/INR, APTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer, troponin, lactate, CRP, and oxygenation monitoring during active storm.
Do not treat aPL serology as the only presentation evidence; use it as confirmatory/context after multiorgan thrombotic presentation is structured.
Actively assess DIC overlap rather than calling all thrombocytopenia plus D-dimer DIC: trend fibrinogen, PT/INR, APTT, bleeding, infection trigger, and organ thrombosis pattern.

Search for and treat triggers: infection cultures/imaging, recent surgery/procedure, malignancy, pregnancy/postpartum complication, lupus flare, medication nonadherence, and anticoagulation interruption.
Organ support: renal replacement therapy when needed, ventilatory support for hypoxemic respiratory failure, vasopressors for shock, cardiac telemetry and echo/troponin follow-up.
Screen for adrenal hemorrhage or adrenal crisis when flank pain, refractory hypotension, hyponatremia/hyperkalemia, or unexplained shock occurs; give stress-dose steroids when clinically indicated.
Use anticoagulation monitoring that accounts for lupus anticoagulant and heparin effects; anti-Xa monitoring may be needed when APTT is unreliable.

Balance anticoagulation against pulmonary hemorrhage, adrenal hemorrhage, ICH, severe thrombocytopenia, and procedures using repeated reassessment rather than stopping thrombosis treatment by default.
Apheresis line placement with bleeding-risk precautions and calcium replacement during plasma exchange.
Vaccination and antimicrobial prophylaxis planning before complement blockade when feasible; urgent therapy may require parallel prophylaxis.
HBV screening and prophylaxis planning before rituximab or high-intensity immunosuppression.
Pregnancy-capable patients need obstetric/rheumatology/hematology co-management; avoid teratogenic transitions when pregnant or actively trying to conceive.
Long-term APS recurrence prevention after stabilization with durable anticoagulation planning, adherence support, and follow-up antibody/thrombotic risk review.
Rehabilitation, wound/vascular surgery, and amputation-prevention care for limb ischemia or cutaneous necrosis survivors.
